summary: Ran cambium's first real end-to-end knowledge cycle on balatron history (distill -> recall -> promote to team -> endorse -> org PR -> cross-project recall). Federation validated: balatron-earned knowledge recalled from the Clark project.
problem: Cambium had never been exercised on a real project's history end to end. We needed to prove the local->team->org promotion lifecycle and, critically, cross-project recall actually work before relying on cambium as the org knowledge layer.
why_chosen: Drove cambium_server.py functions directly (the cambium MCP tools were not exposed in the session) with CAMBIUM_REPO=balatron, CAMBIUM_ORG_REPO=knowledge, org PR mode on. distill() produced 80 items (62 decisions + 18 constraints) entirely from context-keeper; agentsync contributed 0 (see companion constraint). Five standing recall queries, run to cross the recalls>=3 gate, promoted 22 items to the team cambium branch via the worktree+CAS path. con-016 (doc-sync) and con-014 (regime-boundary) were endorsed as universal practice and promoted to org as PRs #1/#2 (since merged). Pointing cambium at the Clark repo with the same org store, both items recalled back stamped project=balatron — the pass condition for compound, cross-project knowledge growth.
what_we_tried: A single pass of the five queries maxed at 2 recalls, so the queries were repeated across 3 rounds to represent recurring usage and cross the promotion gate of 3.
tradeoffs: Two known frictions surfaced (recorded as constraints): cambium's lexical recall missed con-016 for the phrase 'documentation sync rule' (endorsement path used instead of recall), and parallel org PRs conflicted on knowledge.json.

summary: Normalize cp1252 mojibake at the write chokepoint (_new_item), not only in the KNOWLEDGE.md export renderer, so the canonical knowledge.json and recall() serve clean text.
problem: _demojibake ran only in the markdown export path, so distill/import/capture stored substrate content verbatim. A cp1252-mangled em-dash from a source (context-keeper .context/, an import export, an agentsync note) persisted in knowledge.json; recall() reads the store directly, so agents received the mojibake while the exported KNOWLEDGE.md looked clean. Observed live: two org items in jarmstrong158/knowledge carried a broken em-dash in the store while the .md rendered fine.
why_chosen: _new_item is the single normalize-and-write chokepoint every source already routes through (distill agentsync + context-keeper readers, import adapters, manual capture, valid_while premise), so one edit cleans content/why/tags/source.ref for all paths. _demojibake is already guarded (re-decodes only on a tell-tale lead byte AND a clean cp1252->utf-8 round-trip), so correct text and legitimately-accented content are never corrupted. Export keeps its own _demojibake as belt-and-suspenders for pre-existing data.
what_we_tried: Export-only demojibake (the prior state), which left the canonical store and recall() output corrupted while masking the problem in the published doc.
tradeoffs: Repair happens at ingest, so items already corrupted in a store are not retroactively cleaned by this change alone (handled separately by a data fix / re-render). Normalization runs on every write, a negligible cost since the guard short-circuits on pure-ASCII text.

summary: Gate team->org promotion on generalization: a project-specific body is refused at the org boundary unless restated via org_content= (kept concrete as `example`) or forced. Mirrors the endorsement gate; recall surfaces endorsed_as; review_promotions self-reports org_needs_generalization.
problem: promote(to_scope='org') was a pure scope-flag flip that copied the body verbatim. Scopes differ by readership (local=you, org=every project), so a single-repo runbody (names dashboard.py, clark_foundation.pt) promoted unchanged is useless or misleading org-wide, yet gets recalled/cited/institutionalized. The generalization already existed in the endorsement note but recall() buried it in the trust blob, so the right statement was captured and hidden while the wrong one was served.
why_chosen: Follows cambium's existing split (Decision 3): crossing into org is a hard gate, drift within a scope is a soft signal. This is a crossing, so it gets a gate mirroring the endorsement gate exactly (same not_* refusal, same force=True override). cambium stays deterministic/model-free: a regex lint (_org_body_smells_local: origin-project name, filenames, test ids, dec/con refs) detects the smell and hands back the endorsement note as a ready draft; the human restates. org_content becomes the org body and the concrete is preserved as example. Companion moves close the loop: recall surfaces endorsement notes as endorsed_as, and review_promotions reports org_needs_generalization so the tool self-diagnoses runbooks that crossed before the gate. Verified against the live org corpus: flags exactly the 4 project-specific items (plus one that names its own project) and leaves the 4 genuinely-universal ones clean.
what_we_tried: Considered warn-only lint (rejected: contradicts 'don't make the unsafe org path easy') and recall-only surfacing of endorsement notes (rejected as primary: treats the read symptom, leaves promote shipping un-generalized bodies) -- the latter folded in as a supporting move.
tradeoffs: The lint is precision-biased, not exhaustive: a bare word/word 'path' is deliberately NOT a tell (prose uses slashes for lists like survey/claim/update_status, and real paths of concern end in a filename the file-tell catches), so a bare directory path with no filename/project-name can slip through. Accepted because a false block is costlier than a false pass here, and force=True plus the review_promotions backstop catch the remainder.

summary: Add generalize() to remediate org items that crossed before the gate (restate body in place from the endorsement note, keep concrete as example, PR-batched); and make distill fall back why_chosen -> rationale for pre-v0.4 context-keeper decisions.
problem: The generalization gate (dec-003) only prevents FUTURE mis-scoped org crossings; the items already in org before it (5 in the live corpus) still had project-specific bodies with no tool-managed way to fix them — hand-editing knowledge.json was the anti-pattern the user rejected. Separately, the stack integration audit found distill read decision rationale from why_chosen only; context-keeper renamed rationale->why_chosen at v0.4 but still reads both, so a pre-v0.4 decision's entire WHY was silently dropped while its summary was kept.
why_chosen: generalize() is the remediation counterpart of the gate and reuses its parts: it edits a promoted item in place (org via a new _org_mutate_direct/_org_mutate_pr CAS path, team via _team_mutate), defaulting org_content to the item's latest endorsement note (where the restatement already lives), preserving the concrete body as example, and clearing the org_needs_generalization flag; PR mode batches all edits onto one shared cambium/generalize branch so remediation is one reviewable PR. Verified end-to-end: the 5 flagged live items generalized into knowledge#11, detector then clean. The rationale fallback (e.get(why_f) or e.get(\"rationale\")) mirrors context-keeper's own back-compat, one line, no downside.

summary: Make cambium project-aware for the solo-operator-is-org model: CAMBIUM_REPO defaults to the cwd git root when unset, so one config (org_repo + agent_id) serves every project; the SessionEnd hook also reads the session cwd from its payload.
problem: The operator is the org and works across many solo projects; local->team->org collapses to per-project->one shared knowledge brain. A global SessionEnd distill hook pinned to a single CAMBIUM_REPO would only ever capture one project, and interactive recall/promote would target the wrong repo.
why_chosen: Rather than require per-project cambium config, CAMBIUM_REPO falls back to the git root at/above cwd (new _git_root helper) in _cfg and _config_state when set in neither env nor config file. One config sets the stable pieces (CAMBIUM_ORG_REPO = the knowledge repo, CAMBIUM_AGENT_ID); the project is whatever repo the session is in. _config_source reports source 'cwd' so status stays coherent. The SessionEnd hook additionally reads the payload cwd and sets CAMBIUM_REPO (belt-and-suspenders, since the hook process cwd may differ from the session project). Team scope is vestigial for a solo org but harmless. Verified: cambium 63/63, xylem 75/75.

summary: Do not add semantic (embedding) recall to cambium yet. Keep the lexical token-overlap scorer (_score). Re-evaluate when the knowledge base crosses ~100 items using bench_recall.py.
problem: Recall is currently lexical (token overlap), documented in _score as "the semantic upgrade is a later swap." Raised: how hard is semantic recall and is it worth doing now? Needed a data-backed answer before spending effort, and before giving up the zero-dependency property that embeddings would cost.
why_chosen: Ran bench_recall.py against the live 9-item knowledge base with 18 queries (9 control sharing vocabulary, 9 paraphrases using different words). The correct item scored 0.50-1.00 in ALL 18 cases, always far above the 0.2 abstention floor; zero true recall misses. Paraphrase top-1 (89%) equaled control (89%): substring matching plus double-weighted tags close the synonym gap at this scale. The only 2 top-1 failures were the same homonym collision on "sync" (decision-log-sync vs state-mirror-sync), which embeddings do NOT reliably fix and which surface at rank 2 anyway (limit=5). Embeddings would cost a dependency, kill the zero-dependency selling point, force recalibration of the floor, and fix nothing the data shows.
what_we_tried: Built bench_recall.py (in cambium repo) as the repeatable measurement. Considered three embedding approaches: local model (fastembed/ONNX MiniLM ~90MB), embedding API (Voyage/OpenAI; Claude has no embeddings endpoint), and hybrid flag-gated reranking. Hybrid is the preferred approach IF the trigger fires.
tradeoffs: Homonym near-misses (correct item at rank 2) persist for now; mitigated by tag hygiene, not embeddings. Result is sample-size-limited: 9 items is tiny and tag-rich, so the picture changes with more or sloppier entries, hence the explicit re-eval trigger.
constraints_created: Re-run bench_recall.py when the cambium knowledge base crosses ~100 items; build hybrid embedding recall only if paraphrase top-1 drops below ~70% OR a gold item falls below the abstention floor. Homonym collisions alone are not a trigger; fix tags instead.

summary: Added solo/team auto-detection to cambium with a solo fast-lane for org promotion. Detection is automatic and reversible; the generalization gate is never relaxed.
problem: cambium's promotion ladder (local -> team -> org) rests on three trust signals, two of which assume other people: peer endorsement and org PR review. For a solo builder those collapse to self-endorsement and self-reviewed PRs, so the team tier and the mandatory endorsement gate become ceremony with no one to perform them. The user wanted the process to be effective solo WITHOUT removing any team utility.
why_chosen: Detection is inferred, not configured: _detect_mode() counts distinct identities ever seen (configured agent + agentsync claim owners + endorsement by-fields across local/team/org); <=1 is solo. CAMBIUM_MODE=auto|solo|team overrides. In solo mode, promote(item_id, to_scope="org") may originate from LOCAL (skips the team hop) and the deliberate promote call itself counts as the endorsement (auto-stamped {by: agent} for the audit trail). This is purely additive: team mode behavior is byte-identical to before, so nothing is lost when a team exists. It is reversible with zero migration: the day a second collaborator claims or endorses anything, detection flips to team and the full peer-endorsement ladder re-engages. The user chose the "fast lane" option (promote = the vouch) over keeping a separate explicit endorse step.
what_we_tried: Considered a plain CAMBIUM_SOLO flag (rejected: manual, and would collapse the tier rather than adapt). Considered auto-satisfying endorsement in solo mode without allowing the direct local->org hop (that was the runner-up option offered). Chose inference + fast-lane because it grows with the user.
tradeoffs: The one quality bar that is NEVER relaxed is the generalization gate (_org_body_smells_local): a project-specific body still must be restated via org_content before it can reach org, in every mode. So solo speeds up the ceremony but not the abstraction discipline, which is the piece that actually matters for a multi-project solo dev. Cost: _detect_mode does a git fetch of the agentsync branch (acceptable, promote already does git ops).
constraints_created: The solo fast-lane must never relax cambium's generalization gate (_org_body_smells_local): a project-specific body always requires an org_content restatement (or force=True) before promotion to org, regardless of solo/team mode.

summary: Three integrity fixes: (1) local store writes are atomic + corrupt files are quarantined not silently emptied; (2) recall credit is deduped per (agent, UTC day) so a self-recall loop can't inflate trust into promotion; (3) a new deprecate() tool retires items across local/team/org through existing CAS paths.
problem: Audit of cambium found three unguarded gaps not covered by DESIGN/README: _write_local was non-atomic and _read_local returned an empty store on any JSON parse error, so a crash mid-write or one corrupt byte silently destroyed all local (non-git-backed) knowledge on the next write. recall() incremented trust.recalls with no per-agent dedup and 3 recalls auto-qualifies local->team, so one agent looping the same query promotes its own item. And there was no tool to retire wrong/stale knowledge (deprecation was hand-editing JSON), despite stale_report surfacing stale items and the README worrying about wrong knowledge getting institutionalized.
why_chosen: Atomic temp+os.replace with a corrupt-file quarantine turns a silent-total-loss into a recoverable file, and only local needs it (team/org are git-recoverable). Deduping recall credit by (agent, UTC day) kills the trivial self-inflation loop while preserving 'usage promotes' for sustained real use across days or teammates; it also lets recall SKIP the team CAS git-push when there's nothing new to credit, cheapening the hot path without redesigning the push. deprecate() routes through the same local/_team_mutate/_org_mutate paths promotion uses and sets status=deprecated, which recall/export/promotion already filter out - completing the lifecycle stale_report points at. Deliberately did NOT touch _score's substring matching (it feeds bench_recall and needs measurement) or redesign the recall git-push mechanism (owner asked to explain-before-changing that).
tradeoffs: A purely-local item (only ever recalled by its owner) now needs multi-day use OR an endorsement to promote by recalls, not N recalls in one session. recall_marks grows per (agent,day) on each item (bounded, trimmable later). deprecate is retire-only; reactivation stays a manual JSON edit.

summary: _score's >=3-char substring match is now prefix-based (w.startswith(tok) or tok.startswith(w)) instead of bare bidirectional infix (tok in w or w in tok), removing false positives like "art"~"start" while keeping stem/plural matches like hash~hashing.
problem: The lexical scorer credited a query token >=3 chars if it appeared ANYWHERE inside a stored body word (or vice versa). That let unrelated short tokens score hits ("art" in "start", "cat" in "locate"), which both added recall noise and — because recall counts feed promotion — inflated the trust of items that had nothing to do with the query. Flagged in the audit as the precision half of the recall-integrity work; deferred because changing scoring needed measurement.
why_chosen: The intended matches the docstring cites (jwt~jwts, hash~hashing) are all shared-prefix relationships; the false positives are infix/suffix. Requiring one token to be a prefix of the other keeps every intended stem/plural match and drops the spurious ones, with no new dependency. Validated with bench_recall.py against the real org knowledge.json: control top-1 8/9 and paraphrase top-1 8/9 (89%) both unchanged, 0 gold items below the relevance floor before and after; only min-gold moved 0.50->0.40 (a gold item losing a self-inflating infix hit while still ranked #1). So precision improved with recall provably unchanged.
tradeoffs: Prefix matching still allows some loose stems (e.g. "cat"~"category"); tightening further (true stemming) would need a dependency or a stopword/affix list and wasn't justified by the benchmark. bench_recall is still not wired into CI (needs the org fixture); a self-contained _score precision unit test covers the regression in CI instead.

summary: Add a read-only session_primer() tool that returns a compact digest of the current project's highest-value knowledge, for automatic injection at SessionStart via a new xylem hook — making recall passive instead of an advisory step an agent has to remember.
problem: The stack's recall discipline was advisory prose only: SessionStart injected a context-keeper summary but nothing ran cambium, so an agent had to remember to call recall() — and at this session's start it didn't, so cambium was ignored. Capture (SessionEnd distill) is automated; recall was not. The loop was half-open.
why_chosen: A dedicated primer (top active items by recalls then recency across local/team/org, plus stale valid_while assumptions) is what a hook can inject cheaply at session start. It is READ-ONLY — unlike recall() it does NOT increment recall counts — because a passive session-start surfacing must not inflate trust or trigger promotion. The hook (in xylem) resolves the session's real project from the SessionStart payload cwd and points cambium's config file at it, so the per-call-resolving cambium server follows the session project; this is the only one of the three servers that can follow mid-life (context-keeper/agentsync resolve once at startup and need a separate per-call change).
tradeoffs: Primer reads all scopes each session start (a couple of git fetches); acceptable for a once-per-session hook. It ranks by recalls+recency, not query relevance, since there is no query at session start.

summary: distill() now re-syncs source lifecycle: it reads the full context-keeper entry set each run, auto-deprecates LOCAL cambium items whose source decision/constraint became superseded/deprecated, and REPORTS (does not auto-push) promoted team/org copies. It also keeps the decision's `problem` in the distilled `why`, and stops mislabeling a corrupt .context store as read.
problem: Audit found cambium never re-synced a source decision's lifecycle: once distilled while active, a decision that context-keeper later superseded/deprecated stayed active and recallable in cambium and could climb to org, where promotion stamps last_verified so it looks freshly verified — wrong knowledge institutionalized. The decision's `problem` (what forced it) was also dropped, removing the context needed to judge org-worthiness; and a corrupt .context file was reported as 'read'.
why_chosen: Reading the full entry set (not just active) lets one distill pass both import new active entries and expire retired ones. Auto-deprecation is scoped to LOCAL only — where distill already writes — because auto-pushing deprecations to the shared team/org branch from an automatic SessionEnd hook would violate cambium's 'org is a hard gate' rule; promoted stale copies are surfaced as stale_promoted with a suggested deprecate() call for a deliberate act. Folding `problem` into `why` makes it recalled and visible at the promotion gate without a new field. Setting ck_seen only after a successful load stops a corrupt store from looking captured.
tradeoffs: The team/org stale scan does 1-2 extra git reads per distill, but only when some source entry is actually retired. deprecated cambium items remain in the store (filtered from recall/export) for audit; reactivation stays manual.

summary: Rewrote the tool descriptions Glama scored lowest (record_need 3.1, endorse 3.4) to address behavioural disclosure, parameter semantics and when-to-use guidance. Accepted a measured +20% tools/list token cost as a deliberate, bounded trade rather than applying the same treatment catalogue-wide.
problem: Glama grades an MCP server 70% on Tool Definition Quality and 30% on Server Coherence, scoring every tool 1-5 and computing the server score as 60% mean plus 40% MINIMUM, so a single terse tool drags the whole server down. cambium sat at grade A but only 75%, with record_need at 3.1 and endorse at 3.4 named as the weakest. The reported gaps were specific: undisclosed side effects, unexplained optional parameters, and no guidance distinguishing a tool from its neighbours.
why_chosen: The 40% minimum weighting means effort is best spent on the worst tools rather than spread evenly, and Glama names them, so the target list is given rather than guessed. The rewrites deliberately cover the non-obvious behaviours an agent would otherwise get wrong: endorse appends a SECOND stamp rather than replacing the first, record_need does not deduplicate, and nothing leaves the local scope until promote is called. That is the same information that makes the tool safer to use, so the Glama score and real usability point the same way here.
what_we_tried: Checked first whether a schema token budget applied. The string 'Keep the schema under 2500 tokens per TestToolSchemaBudget' appears in test_cambium.py but is FIXTURE DATA for a test about the enforced_by field format, not an actual budget test - cambium has no TestToolSchemaBudget. The real ceiling is context-keeper's con-004, which is why context-keeper was left alone. Measured the cost after the rewrite: cambium's tools/list went from ~4505 to ~5403 estimated tokens.
tradeoffs: Tool descriptions load into model context at every session start, so this is a permanent per-session token tax on every user, measured at +20% for cambium. Justified for five high-misuse tools; explicitly NOT a licence to enrich every tool, which would roughly double the payload for diminishing score gains.

alternatives.option: Enrich every tool description to maximise the mean
alternatives.reason_rejected: The score weights the minimum at 40%, so the worst tools dominate; enriching already-strong tools (several score 4.8-5.0) buys little and doubles the per-session token cost.

alternatives.option: Apply the same rewrite to context-keeper
alternatives.reason_rejected: It is already grade A and is governed by con-004, a test-enforced ceiling on the tools/list payload with thin headroom.

constraints_created: Before enriching an MCP tool description for score reasons, measure the tools/list token delta and justify it per tool. Verbosity is a per-session cost paid by every user, and Glama's scoring weights the minimum tool at 40%, so only the weakest tools are worth the tax.

summary: cambium/tools/dashboard.py renders the whole memory mesh as one self-contained local HTML: every project's context-keeper log plus the cambium layer distilled from them, across four views (distillation funnel, per-project drill-in, knowledge/promotion ladder, health as a share of each population). Local and gitignored by design; read-only, asserted byte-for-byte.
problem: Counting entries was already possible -- the Xylem dashboard reports per-store dec/con counts across 34 projects -- but nothing showed what was INSIDE a store or anything at all about cambium's knowledge, which appeared only as a component tile with a number. The first run answered a question no single tool could, and the answer inverted the naive reading: local scope holds 229 items with 15 recalled (7%), while TEAM scope holds 136 items with 134 recalled (99%) and 774 recalls. Promotion is what makes knowledge get read; local is a staging area and its low recall rate is the system working. That conclusion is only visible with both scopes in one view. It also surfaced 84 items carrying cp1252 mojibake distilled out of stores before context-keeper fixed the transport -- concentrated on the team branches that are recalled most.
why_chosen: One artifact for two levels, because they are two questions about the same data: per-repo answers 'what did we decide here and is it still true', the overview answers 'is the knowledge layer earning its keep'. Splitting them into separate tools would have duplicated the collection layer and made the funnel -- which only means anything when you can see both ends -- impossible to draw. LOCAL rather than published is the load-bearing choice: the mesh spans private repos and ones with no remote at all, so a published version could honestly show aggregates and nothing else (con-015-12da), whereas a local one shows entry text, scopes and health per project. Health figures are reported as a share of the population they are drawn from rather than as raw counts, so a large store does not read as unhealthy merely for being large. The tool reads .context/ and .cambium/ as plain JSON and imports neither server, so it runs whatever state those are in -- including a half-written file, which is a normal state for a live store and is covered by a test. Stdlib only, matching the rest of the suite.
what_we_tried: The first version read .cambium/knowledge.json only and reported '0 promoted, nothing has left local' -- a real reporting bug, because that file holds LOCAL scope and team knowledge lives on a `cambium` git branch. It produced exactly the wrong headline (a 93%-write-only knowledge layer) and I reported it twice before a check of the shared branches contradicted it. _read_team now reads the branch via `git show`, trying the local ref then the fetched remote one, and never fetching -- a dashboard must not block on the network. Earlier, extending the existing Xylem dashboard was considered and rejected: it is regenerated by an automated workflow from the remote Workers, so a panel fed by local files would be overwritten, and it is published, which caps what it could honestly show to aggregates.
tradeoffs: Being local means it cannot be linked or shared, and it sees only what this machine has fetched -- team scope is read from whatever the last `git fetch` brought down, so it can lag. The output is a single ~300KB file with all entry text embedded, fine at 400 entries and needing paging well before it became a problem. Entry text is truncated to 240 characters, so the view is for orientation and triage, not for reading a decision's full rationale. And the team-branch mojibake it surfaces cannot be fixed by tools/repair_mojibake.py, which deliberately refuses to rewrite shared git history from a maintenance script.

alternatives.option: A panel on the existing Xylem dashboard
alternatives.reason_rejected: It is regenerated by an automated workflow from the remote Workers, so locally-sourced content would be clobbered; and it is published, which caps what it could honestly show to aggregates.

alternatives.option: Two separate tools, one per level
alternatives.reason_rejected: Duplicates the collection layer, and the distillation funnel only means anything when both ends are visible in one place.

alternatives.option: Publish it as a GitHub Pages site like context-keeper's project page
alternatives.reason_rejected: The mesh includes private repos and projects with no remote. A public version could show aggregates only, which is precisely the detail that makes it useful.

alternatives.option: Import context-keeper's mojibake/scope_rules modules rather than inlining the markers
alternatives.reason_rejected: A cross-repo import makes the tool fail when the sibling checkout is absent or mid-refactor -- exactly when you most want to look at the stores.

constraints_created: A tool that reads project memory must be provably read-only -- test_dashboard.py compares every store file byte-for-byte before and after a build.
dashboard.html is generated and gitignored; it must never be committed, because it embeds entry text from private projects.

summary: Pages are a build-artifact tier stored in .cambium/pages.json, isolated from every trust-tier read by file separation, with staleness computed from a per-source content hash rather than timestamps.
problem: cambium needed a synthesis layer that compiles readable pages from context-keeper entries, but a derived summary that could be recalled, promoted or cited would let a lossy restatement outrank the entries it came from and climb to org scope. Separately, "is this page still true" had no honest answer: entries carry created_at/updated_at/verified_at/status but no revision counter, so there was nothing to compare a compile against.
why_chosen: Isolation is structural instead of a rule anyone has to remember: every trust-tier read (recall, session_primer, export_markdown, stale_report, review_promotions) iterates data["items"] in knowledge.json, so putting pages in a different file makes them unreachable by construction, and cambium's existing refusal to write .context/ keeps them out of reload_constraints for free. Deleting pages.json loses nothing because every page rebuilds from .context/ alone. For staleness, the content hash is authoritative and updated_at only corroborates, because timestamp error is real in BOTH directions in these stores: they are documented as human-editable JSON and are edited by hand, so a body changes with no bump, while _backfill_updated_at stamps updated_at onto entries that never changed. A fifth cause, new_match, exists because a tag page is most often wrong by omission and no per-source diff can see a newly recorded entry that belongs on the page. compiled_at sits outside the identity hash so an unchanged store recompiles byte-identically, the same choice context-keeper made in export_snapshot for the same git-churn reason.
what_we_tried: The first implementation re-ran the selector for every page kind, so index and unfiled pages fell through _select_entries' "no tag, no topic, so match everything" branch and reported every active entry as a new match. Seven pages came out stale the instant they were compiled, and only the real stores showed it - the seeded test store was too small. Fixed with _selector_matches returning None for selectors that are not a function of entries, plus a regression test. The unfiled selector also had to record the cluster floor it was built with, since min_cluster=3 yields a different uncovered set than the default and would otherwise report drift that never happened.
tradeoffs: Pages read all three entry kinds including pipelines, so the page tier is deliberately a superset of what distill imports as knowledge - one more place the two can diverge. Hashing all non-excluded fields means a future schema field makes every page stale, chosen as the safe failure direction but it will cause a one-off mass recompile.
constraints_created: Pages must never be written into .context/ or knowledge.json

summary: The mesh dashboard is served from the operator's own machine over Tailscale, not GitHub Pages, and both snapshot.json and pages.json are gitignored. Projects come from an explicit CAMBIUM_PROJECTS map, never a filesystem scan.
problem: The dashboard needs the full cross-project mesh to be useful, but that data spans 20 stores on this machine including a private repo and one with no remote. The original plan was to commit the snapshot and deploy the site to GitHub Pages, which collides head-on with con-015-12da in context-keeper and with the reasoning behind gitignoring dashboard.html here.
why_chosen: Making the repo private does not solve it: a GitHub Pages site built from a private repo is still a publicly reachable website, since access-controlled Pages is a GitHub Enterprise Cloud feature. So the choice was between a hosted surface with auth in front of it and serving from the machine that already holds the data. Tailscale wins because the data never leaves the desktop at all, which means no new exposure surface to reason about and no amendment to con-015-12da - the constraint is honoured in both its letter and its stated reason rather than worked around. tailscale serve also issues a real HTTPS certificate on the tailnet, which is exactly what a service worker and Add to Home Screen require, so the privacy-preserving option is also the one that makes it installable as a phone app. The cost is that the desktop must be awake to serve, accepted knowingly. The explicit project map follows the same principle at the read end: a filesystem scan silently pulls in private and local-only stores, whereas a name someone typed cannot surprise them, and projects named but missing a store are reported as skipped rather than being silently absent.
what_we_tried: GitHub Pages from a private repo was the original request and was rejected once the public-site behaviour was confirmed. A Cloudflare Worker behind Cloudflare Access was the other serious option and fits the existing Worker variants in this suite, but it puts the entire cross-project memory at rest in Cloudflare, which is a real exposure change for a personal tool whose whole point is that the data is private.
tradeoffs: No access when the desktop is off or off the tailnet, and no public demo of the dashboard. The snapshot cannot be committed to either public repo, so cross-machine sync needs a private repo (jarmstrong158/knowledge, already private and already cambium's org store) with Pages left disabled.

summary: Pages synthesize by traversing the entry graph (resolved references, supersession as change history, cross-entry tension detection), structured by role rather than file order — and stay deterministic and model-free.
problem: The first page tier grouped entries by tag, sorted by id, bolded field names and appended a source list. Every sentence was copied verbatim from a single entry, related_to rendered as a bare id, and supersession did not appear at all. Challenged directly on whether this was synthesis or just a log, the honest answer was that it was selection plus formatting - a log with a table of contents - and that no page said anything that was not already in one entry.
why_chosen: The material for real synthesis was already in the stores and simply unread: related_to, constraints_created, enforced_by and superseded_by form a graph whose every edge was an inert id in the JSON. Resolving those edges produces statements no single entry contains - a rule naming the decision that created it, a change line quoting what a decision replaced and why it moved. Structuring by role (rules in force, then how it got decided, then what changed) is a genuine restructure of the material rather than a reordering, because it answers the questions in the order someone actually asks them. Staying deterministic and model-free was the load-bearing constraint: a model writing the prose would break delete-and-rebuild (the body would no longer be regenerable from entries alone) and would make staleness undecidable, since a rebuild that differs could mean the sources moved or merely that the model rephrased. Tension detection is limited to two checks - a reference pointing at an id not in the store, and entries sharing tags with no link either way - because anything verify_quality already judges must be left to it; two tools computing one judgement is how they come to disagree.
what_we_tried: Rendering arcs forced sources to carry a role. Quoting a superseded predecessor means the page contains text from an entry the selector never chose, and marking those as ordinary sources made every page with any history permanently stale, since a predecessor is superseded by definition. Context sources fix it: content hashed (an edit to quoted text really does change what the page says) but status not treated as a cause. That established the invariant that every entry the body renders must be a tracked source, asserted by a test that scrapes entry ids out of the rendered markdown. Separately, the unlinked-pair heuristic counted the page's own selector tag toward shared tags, which every entry on a tag page shares by construction, turning a >=2 threshold into >=1 and flagging 143 of 221 real pages; excluding the selector tag brought it to 92, which is a true property of these stores rather than an artifact.
tradeoffs: Synthesis quality is bounded by how well the stores are linked, and this mesh has 422 entries with 2 supersession edges and few related_to links - so the change-history sections are nearly empty today and the payoff grows only as linking improves. Deterministic synthesis can assemble and restructure but cannot summarize or reconcile in prose, which is the ceiling until and unless a separate model-written tier is added with its own contract.

summary: Pages get a reading surface via export_pages (an Obsidian vault), link backfill becomes automatic by running context-keeper's survey on every snapshot, and related-page links mean shared entries rather than same project.
problem: Three gaps were left after the synthesis rewrite. Pages were worth reading but nothing read them - they existed only as JSON, and the dashboard showed counts rather than bodies. The supersession backfill required remembering to run a script, so it never happened, leaving 423 entries with 2 supersession edges and starving the synthesis of the graph it traverses. And every page linked to every sibling in its project.
why_chosen: The wikilinks the pages already emit are Obsidian's [[slug]] format, so writing one file per page named after its slug turns the existing output into a navigable vault with working backlinks and zero new UI - the reading surface was one export away rather than a feature. Frontmatter doubles as Obsidian Properties so the vault is queryable without the body carrying metadata. For the backfill, automatic means automatically PROPOSED, never automatically applied: context-keeper's survey script is read-only by deliberate design because an edge written from a heuristic silently demotes a rule that may still be in force, so cambium runs it on every snapshot and surfaces the result in the dashboard where the user already looks, leaving the judgement human. It is delegated rather than reimplemented because the script scores pairs with the same function the write-time advisory uses, and a second implementation would drift until the two disagreed about what same subject means. On the third point, linking every sibling produced 17488 wikilinks across 221 pages, roughly 79 per page, which is a hairball in a vault graph and noise in a backlinks panel; overlap-based linking gives 2099 with none broken. Same lesson as the tension heuristic earlier in the session - a signal that fires everywhere is not a signal, and a link that is always present says nothing.
what_we_tried: export_pages reaps orphaned files from its output directory so a deleted page cannot linger, but reaping in a directory a human may also use is dangerous, so every generated file carries a marker in its frontmatter and only marked files are ever deleted - verified by a test that drops a hand-written note in the vault and asserts it survives a re-export. The export is also byte-stable (no compiled_at in frontmatter) so a vault kept in git does not churn.
tradeoffs: The vault contains full entry prose from every named project, so it is gitignored for the same reason as the snapshot. The link survey scans by root, so it reads more stores than are named; only named projects are surfaced, which keeps the explicit-map promise at the output boundary rather than the read boundary.

summary: A concept tier sits above the page tier: cross-project laws written by judgement, whose staleness against the corpus is computed. It is the dashboard's landing view, and one `refresh` command keeps every derived surface current.
problem: The page tier synthesized per-tag-per-project, which is the wrong axis for the question the whole system exists to answer - "what have we learned across everything". There was no collective view, the synthesis lived in a vault file the user had to remember to open rather than in the dashboard, and every iteration required the user to ask for it. The LLM-wiki pattern names the gap: entity pages per CONCEPT drawn across all sources, with an incremental compile that reads new material against the existing wiki.
why_chosen: The split that makes this work without a model is that writing a law takes judgement while detecting that it has fallen behind is a comparison. A law carries topic tags; the exporter finds every entry in the mesh carrying two or more of them, subtracts the ids the law already cites, and what remains is the next compile's work list - generated with nobody noticing it was needed, which is what "it should iterate by itself" actually requires. Two-or-more rather than any is load-bearing: single-tag matching flagged all 17 laws as behind, and a work list that fires on everything is not one, which is the corpus's own rule about detectors. Laws live in cambium's knowledge store rather than a document because the store is the authority and recall() already serves it to any agent in any project, so a future session gets "systems fail by proceeding, not crashing" before it writes code rather than after. _LESSONS.md became a generated projection of that store for the same reason a constraint must not restate a number its test owns - it had been hand-maintained for exactly one session before becoming a second copy that would drift silently. Revisions go through deprecate plus recapture rather than in-place edits, which leaves the supersession record this mesh almost entirely lacks.
what_we_tried: The first compile pass ran end to end and moved 17 laws / 5 behind to 19 / 5, with two new laws that the evidence forced (CI on one machine is observation not verification; a CI config matching no branch is indistinguishable from one that passes). Three of this session's own bugs were instances of laws written minutes earlier: refresh reported laws_behind zero because it recomputed against an empty corpus, a check that could only ever return clean; the generated markdown looked corrupted only because it was inspected with PowerShell Get-Content, which reads BOM-less UTF-8 as cp1252 exactly as con-005 describes; and sharpening the candidate rule broke the test whose fixture encoded the old single-tag behaviour, caught only by the full suite because the targeted subsets filtered that test out by name.
tradeoffs: Deterministic detection cannot judge which candidates actually belong in a law, so the compile pass still needs an agent; the mechanism only guarantees the work list exists and is ranked. Tag-overlap is a proxy for relevance and will miss an entry that belongs but is tagged differently. Laws sit at local scope, so recall() serves them only inside cambium until they are promoted to org - a gate that deliberately requires a human endorsement.
